# OA.2 Argentina {#arg}

Section 5 of the paper calibrates the model with informal households to Argentina before the coverage reforms and
reads the reforms as a rise of the universal pension $\epsilon$; appendix D gives the survey, the identifying
formulas and the sources. This chapter holds the calibration under both treatments of the taste for leisure, the
reform at every intertemporal elasticity of the model's grid, the equilibrium over pension designs, and the
calibration at every IES.

## OA.2.1 Calibration {#arg-calibration}

The paper takes the taste for leisure common to the four formal quartiles and pins its level by the average formal
workweek, so relative hours are a prediction. The alternative identifies one $X_i$ per quartile from the survey's
relative hours. Only the productivity and leisure parameters differ between the two: the aggregate targets, and
every result of section 5, are the same under both.

{{< include _generated/groups/arg-calibration.qmd >}}

## OA.2.2 The reform {#arg-reform}

The first table is the paper's: the effect in 2010 of raising $\epsilon$ to the universal level, with the tax rate
held at its pre-reform path and chosen politically. The second prints the paths of the tax rate, the savings rate
and the workweek before and after the reform.

{{< include _generated/groups/arg-reform.qmd >}}

## OA.2.3 The reform across the intertemporal elasticity {#arg-rho}

Section 5 reads the reform across the intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES) $\rho$ from the figure, which
is the paper's; the model is solved on a grid of sixteen values. The table prints the reform at every point of the
grid. [Click a point of the figure for its row.]{.content-visible when-format="html"}

{{< include _generated/groups/arg-rho.qmd >}}

## OA.2.4 The equilibrium over pension designs {#arg-designs}

The equilibrium in 2010 over a grid of designs $(\epsilon, \theta)$, each point an economy that has always had that
design, with the pre-reform calibration and the universal system at the calibrated $\theta$ marked. The tax rate
rises with $\epsilon$ and falls with $\theta$, the savings rate and the workweek fall with $\epsilon$ and rise with
$\theta$, and the savings of informal relative to formal households fall with $\epsilon$. Between the two markers
the tax rate rises by more than it does on impact in section 5 of the paper, because the savings of informal
households have adjusted to the universal system; the difference is close to the reform's effect by 2040 (OA.2.2).
[The grid itself can be downloaded from the figure's source.]{.content-visible when-format="html"}

{{< include _generated/groups/arg-designs.qmd >}}

## OA.2.5 The calibration across the intertemporal elasticity {#arg-rhogrid}

The table and the figure print the parameters solved jointly with the equilibrium path at every IES of the grid,
which show how the calibration absorbs a change in $\rho$: matching the targets at an IES of 0.6 or below takes a
thirty-year discount factor above one.
